October 6, 1915. J. Williar Sheetz may be appointed to a clerkship in the classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with ecivil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Sheetz has served for a number of years as private secretary to the Director of the Mint, has rendered very efficient service, and on account of his knowledge of the mint work it is desired to use his services in a classified position. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order.

December 30, 1922. # Mrs. Anna M. Curran may be reappointed as printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing of the Treasury Department. She served in this position from September 15, 1919, when she was appointed without examination under author- ity of an Executive order of January 15, 1918, until August 13, 1921, when she was furloughed because of reduction of force, her furlough being largely due to the fact that her husband was employed in the Government service. Since her furlough she has been left a widow by the assassination of her husband. She received several bullet wounds in trying to protect him. She has been out of the service too long to be eligible for reemployment, and the Executive order under which she received Shpoigimeit has been revoked. She could have remained in the service indefinitely if no occasion had arisen to require her separation. In view of all the circumstances the Secretary of the Treasury recommends her reinstatement. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation that she be reap- pointed with the same status she would have had if she had remained in the service under her original appointment. Mrs. Curran has been employed in the Government Printing Office since April 2, 1898.

October 10, 1916. Mrs. Vera A. Hardie may be reinstated as a printer ’s assistant in the Bureau of En- _graving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. Mrs. Hardie was appointed on November 1, 1913, and rendered very efficient service until the date of her resignation on account of marriage on April 2, 1915. She has an invalid husband and infant dependent upon her. The Acting Secretary of the Treasury recommended the issuance of this order and the Civil Service Commis- sion concurs in view of Mrs. Hardie’s good record and the short period which has elapsed since her separation from the service.

September 7, 1912. Mr. James B. Brunemer may be appointed a watchman in the Government Printing Office. He is a veteran of the Civil War and served as a watchman in the Post Office Department and later as a clerk in the Treasury and Interior Departments. He is eligible for reinstatement under the rules in any of these departments because of his former service therein; but not in the Government Printing Office. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Public Printer, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, as there are no eligible applicants among the veterans employed in the Government Printing Office. This action merely permits reinstate- ment in an office other than one for which the applicant is already eligible.

October 29, 1913. William A. Ryan may be appointed to the position of comptroller (in charge of all finances and accounting) in the Reclamation Service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, and is based upon Mr. Ryan’s un- usual qualifications for the position and the close personal relationship which he will bear to the Secretary of the Interior. Mr. Ryan has been in the employ of the Inter- state Commerce Commission during the past six years assigned to the duty of examining the books and accounts of transportation companies, and conducted a notable investi- gation which covered a period of three years. He is thoroughly familiar with large financial affairs, it having been his business for several years to draft the plans for the financing of great industrial corporations, and moreover he has an intimate personal knowledge of irrigation experiments and projects. He has been known to the Secre- tary of the Interior for 25 years, and knows his attitude so perfectly that he will be able to state his policies and deal with the more than 20,000 water users without embarrassment to the Secretary.

March 22, 1917. Otto Lewis Evans, of Amherst, Va., a law graduate of the University of Virginia, and a practicing lawyer from 1885 to 1915, and who has served in the Department of State since August 1916, may be appointed a law clerk in the Department of State without reference to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This action is based upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State, because of jhe efficient service of Mr. Evans, and his special qualifications and experience as a awyer.

May 2, 1925. Mrs. Bessie L. Dudley may be appointed in the classified service of the Treas- ury Department without regard to her standing on the eligible register. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that she is the daughter of a former officer in the United States Revenue Cutter Service and a widow with a family of small children to support. The Civil Service Commission submits the order without prejudice but is without authority to recommend its issuance. Done for charity. Her father served in the Navy Department from 1871 to 1899.

July 19, 1916. Mr, Arthur E. Wilson may be permanently appointed to a clerical position in the office of the Surgeon General, Public Health Service, without reference to civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Wilson was appointed a temporary clerk at $1,200 per annum on January 20, 1916, in the Surgeon General's office, to fill a vacancy caused by the resignation of a regular employee on account of illness; that he has given complete satisfaction and has exhibited special capacity for the particular duties assigned to him, which renders his services of peculiar value; and that it is believed Mr. Wilson’s permanent appointment will be in the interest of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

April 14, 1914. Mrs. Ada M. Nolan may be reinstated in the subclerical grade in the classified civil gervice of the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury in view of the excellent record of Mrs. Nolan when formerly in the service of the Treasury Department and in view of the fact that her husband died recently from tuberculosis, leaving his widow with two small children with no means of support. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case. April 22, 1914. ‘ Mr. James W. Cole may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of his separation from that service. Mr. Cole was appointed on March 6, 1901, a regular clerk, and served continuously until July 30, 1910, upon one of the heavy lines of the Railway Mail Service. His record was good. On the latter date, while on duty, he was seriously injured in a wreck and although he has now entirely recovered, he did not recover sufficiently during the period of eligibility fixed by the civil-service rules to permit his reinstate- ment. He was thus forced out of the service by an injury incurred in the line of duty. In view of these facts and of the statement of the department that his reinstatement will bein the interests of the service, the commission concurs with the department in recommending an Executive order.

The requirement of the United States citizenship is hereby waived to permit the certification of Mr. Cedric R. August 3, 1914. _ Mr. Fred T. Karr may be reinstated as a railway postal clerk without reference to the year limit of eligibility.
